title: Data Thinking, Part 5: Telling a story with data - from a table to a decision
subtitle: How to structure an analytical presentation, and why the conclusion belongs on the first slide rather than the last
whyItMatters: An analysis that is correct but that nobody acts on creates no value at all. Most data people spend almost all of their effort finding the answer and almost none on making that answer heard and believed.
openingQuestion: When presenting analytical results to senior management, where should you start?
openingOptions: With the method and data sources, so the audience trusts the reliability first
With the conclusion and the recommendation, and only then the evidence
With the most striking chart, to capture attention
With the broad market context, narrowing down from there
explanation: The order in which you build an analysis and the order in which you present it are two different things, and confusing them is the most common mistake there is. You worked from data to method to conclusion, so you tend to retell it in exactly that order. But the audience needs the conclusion first in order to have a frame for everything that follows. In many meetings you genuinely have only three minutes - and if those three minutes go on method, the conclusion never gets heard at all.

diagram.label: Appendix for anyone who wants to dig

realWorldExample.company: Two ways of presenting the same receivables analysis
realWorldExample.description: The first: fifteen slides opening with data sources, cleaning method, distribution charts, and a recommendation only on the last slide. The meeting ran out of time at slide nine. The second: the first slide carries one sentence - propose tightening credit limits for the customer group more than 60 days past due, estimated to cut bad debt by 12bn a year. Three slides of evidence follow. The method becomes an appendix. The decision was made in twenty minutes.

quiz.question: Why should the conclusion go at the front of a presentation?
options: Because a conclusion is usually short, which suits the opening of a long presentation
Because the audience needs a frame in order to judge the evidence that follows
Because detailed evidence presented too early will cause the audience to lose focus
Because arranging it this way reduces the total number of slides you have to build
quiz.explanation: Without a conclusion to lead the way, listeners have to guess which argument each number is serving. That is an unnecessary burden and it usually ends in a misreading. The other explanations describe side effects rather than reasons: brevity and slide count are not why the order works, and a well-chosen piece of evidence does not cost you attention when the audience already knows what it is for.

quiz.question: Why state the limitations of an analysis instead of hiding them?
options: Because professional standards require every analytical report to include a limitations section
Because a limitations section usefully pads out a presentation when the evidence is thin
Because the audience will find them anyway, and naming them first strengthens everything else
Because stating limitations lets the analyst avoid responsibility if the conclusion is later wrong
quiz.explanation: Experienced listeners always hunt for the weak point. If they find one you did not mention, everything else is immediately suspect - including the parts that were sound. No professional standard mandates the section, it is not padding, and it certainly does not transfer responsibility: naming a limitation is how you keep authority over the argument, not how you give it away.

quiz.question: How many main messages should a single slide carry?
options: Three to five, to use the available space fully and cut the total number of slides needed
Exactly one, and the slide title should be that message rather than the chart type
As many as possible, provided each message comes with specific supporting figures
There is no rule, because this depends entirely on the habits of each organisation
quiz.explanation: Making the title the message instead of a description of the chart is the smallest change with the largest effect. People skimming a deck read only the titles, so written that way they still receive the whole argument. Packing several messages onto one slide forces the reader to work out which is the point, and 'it depends on the organisation' is how decks end up with no standard at all.

quiz.question: When the recommendation runs against what the audience expects, what should you do?
options: State the conclusion clearly, and also present the evidence for the old view and why it falls short
Soften the conclusion so as to avoid a direct confrontation with an existing view
Present all the raw figures and let the audience draw their own conclusions
Postpone the presentation until more data supporting the new conclusion is available
quiz.explanation: Showing that you genuinely weighed their position is the condition for the conclusion being heard at all. Skip the opposing argument and the audience concludes you never considered it, which is a cheaper objection than engaging with your evidence. Softening, stalling, and dumping raw data all avoid the confrontation rather than winning it.

quiz.question: Your recommendation runs against what the audience expects. What is the right way to present it?
options: Lead with the recommendation, exactly as in any other presentation
Build the strongest evidence first, then state the recommendation
Present both options and let the audience choose between them
Send the material in advance so they can prepare themselves
quiz.explanation: Conclusion-first is the general rule, but it has an exception: when the audience already holds the opposite belief, stating the conclusion first triggers rebuttal before they have heard any evidence. Build the evidence first so they arrive at the conclusion alongside you rather than defending a position against it.

keyTakeaways: The order you built the analysis in is not the order to present it - do not retell it as you did it
Conclusion and recommendation first, method moved to the appendix
The slide title is the message, not the name of the chart
State the limitations before the audience finds them
Present the opposing argument too, especially when the conclusion runs against expectations

practicePrompt.question: You have 30 seconds in a lift to report your analysis to the director. What should you say?
options: Describe the method and data sources used, to establish that it is reliable
One sentence of conclusion with the impact figure, and one on what needs deciding
Propose scheduling a separate meeting to present the full findings
Recount the most surprising thing you found during the analysis
practicePrompt.explanation: The lift test is the best way to find out whether you actually understand your own result. If you cannot compress it into two sentences, it is usually because you have not decided what the most important thing is. The second sentence - what needs deciding - is the one that turns a piece of information into an action.

summary.keyIdea: The audience needs the conclusion first in order to have a frame for the evidence that follows
summary.commonMistake: Retelling the analysis in the order you did it, leaving the conclusion on the last slide
summary.action: Write the conclusion as a single sentence before building any slides. If you cannot, the analysis is not finished.

application.title: What to do
application.message: Take a report you once produced and rewrite it in four parts: one sentence of conclusion with a figure, three principal pieces of evidence, the limitations, and an appendix. Compare it against the original to see which parts were actually necessary.
application.secondary: Then retitle every chart, from the name of the chart type to the message that chart proves.

sections.text: Most of a data person's effort goes into finding the right answer. But the value only appears at the final step: when somebody changes a decision because of your result.

sections.title: The four layers of an analytical presentation
sections.subtitle: Ordered as you present them, which is the reverse of the order you worked in

concepts.def: One sentence, with a figure and a recommended action. This is the only part guaranteed to be heard if the meeting gets cut short.
Three main supports, one slide each, with the title as the message rather than the name of the chart. Three is the number people can hold.
What this analysis cannot answer, and which assumptions are holding the conclusion up. Volunteering them is far stronger than being asked.
Method, data sources, alternative cuts of the data. For anyone who wants to verify - and it has to exist, because someone will ask.

sections.label: The title is the message
sections.text: Changing a slide title from Revenue by quarter to Q4 revenue fell 8% on the enterprise customer segment is the smallest change with the largest payoff. The reason is simple: a great many people only skim a deck and read the titles. If those titles join up into a complete argument, they get the whole thing without you standing there to explain it.

left.label: A weak presentation
left.text: Starts with the method. Slide titles describe the chart type. Every finding is given equal weight. Nothing is said about limitations. It ends with a call for further analysis.

right.label: A strong presentation
right.text: Conclusion on the first slide with the impact figure. Three pieces of evidence in clear priority. Limitations and assumptions stated upfront. It ends with a specific proposal that needs a decision.

sections.title: Ask AI to build an inverted-pyramid deck
sections.task: Q4 revenue fell 8%, mostly in enterprise customers. Assemble a prompt for the AI to write the slide titles. Pick one option for each part.

options.text: Say the audience is the board and they must decide whether to raise enterprise sales budget
options.feedback: There is an audience and a decision to make, so the AI knows which recommendation the conclusion must lead to.

options.text: Send the Q4 revenue table and ask for professional-looking slide content
options.feedback: Only data, no audience and no decision. The AI will describe the numbers rather than lead to an action.

options.text: Say the boss is very busy so the deck should be short and pretty, nothing more
options.feedback: Short and pretty is not context. The AI does not know what the boss must decide, so the deck lacks a focus.

options.text: Write three titles that are messages with numbers, forming one argument
options.feedback: Someone skimming only the titles still gets the whole argument, as the lesson said.

options.text: Write three short titles named after the chart, like Revenue by quarter
options.feedback: A title that names the chart type does not tell the reader what to conclude.

options.text: Write lots of catchy titles so I can pick my favourite
options.feedback: Many titles do not make one argument, and every finding is stated at the same weight.

options.text: Add one slide stating what the analysis cannot answer and the assumption propping up the conclusion
options.feedback: Stating limits yourself beats being asked, and it matches the limits tier of the four-tier structure.

options.text: Drop the limitations entirely so the deck is shorter and sounds surer
options.feedback: The audience will ask anyway and you lose the initiative. This is a sign of a weak presentation.

options.text: Just add a methods section at the end for anyone who wants to read it
options.feedback: Methods belong in the appendix. It does not say what was left out or which assumption holds the conclusion up.

responses.text: Title 1: Q4 revenue fell 8%, almost all of it in enterprise customers. Title 2: This segment lost new customers, not existing ones. Title 3: Recommend raising enterprise sales budget; decision needed today. Last slide: the effect of pricing is not analysed, and the conclusion assumes new customers are the main cause.

Title 1: Q4 revenue fell 8%, concentrated in enterprise customers. Title 2: Lost new customers, not existing ones. Title 3: Recommend raising enterprise sales budget. No slide mentions the limits of the analysis, so the audience will ask on their own.
Title 1: Q4 revenue fell 8%. Title 2: One customer group was hit hardest. Title 3: Needs further review. Without an audience and a decision, it ends on a line that says more analysis is needed.
Slide 1: Revenue by quarter. Slide 2: Revenue by customer group. Slide 3: Revenue by region. These are chart-name titles; a skimmer cannot conclude anything.

sections.title: The meeting is cut to five minutes: the deck must still reach a decision

steps.label: Minute one: a conclusion with a number
steps.detail: Open with one sentence: Q4 revenue fell 8%, almost all in enterprise customers, and we recommend raising that segment's sales budget. If the meeting stops here, the audience still has something to decide on.

steps.label: Minutes two and three: three supports
steps.detail: One piece of evidence per slide, each title a message. Someone skimming only the titles can still read a continuous argument from top to bottom.

steps.label: Minute four: the limits you state yourself
steps.detail: The analysis has not answered the effect of pricing, and it assumes new customers are the cause. Stating it first means the audience does not make you defend it.

steps.label: Minute five: the recommendation to decide
steps.detail: End on a concrete choice for the decision-maker, not on a line saying more analysis is needed. The appendix waits for anyone asking about methods or other ways to slice the data.

lines: An analysis nobody acts on produces, in outcome terms, exactly what an analysis never done would have produced.
The last lesson of this stage covers the obligations that come with the work: ethics and risk in working with data.
